Q1022.t: A city poured into a bowl of vineyards
Q1022.s: Stuttgart looks poured into a bowl. Its centre fills a steep hollow that locals call the Kessel, 'the cauldron', while the suburbs spill over the wooded rim and down to the Neckar. Look at the sunny slopes: those neat striped terraces are vineyards, many of them inside the city limits. Wine has been made here for centuries.
Q1022.w: A dense centre in a wooded hollow, the Neckar curving past to the east, striped vineyards on the slopes.
f: Both Mercedes-Benz and Porsche have their headquarters in Stuttgart.
In 1885 Gottlieb Daimler's garden workshop in Cannstatt, now part of Stuttgart, produced one of the first motorcycles.
The mineral springs of Bad Cannstatt are among the most abundant in Europe.

q.q: Which river flows through Stuttgart?

Q588.t: Where a dozen towns have grown into one
Q588.s: Here the towns have run out of gaps between them. Katowice is the hub of the Upper Silesian conurbation, where more than a dozen cities merge into one mesh of housing estates, rail yards and old pitheads. Small ponds dot the patchwork: many fill hollows where the ground sank over worked-out coal seams. To the south, green Beskid ridges close the view.
Q588.w: A sprawling grey-green urban mesh with scattered ponds and rail lines; wooded Beskid hills rise to the south.
f: Katowice received town rights only in 1865, as coal was turning Upper Silesia into an industrial powerhouse.
The Vistula, Poland's longest river, rises on Barania Góra in the Silesian Beskids, about 70 km to the south.
Silesian Park in neighbouring Chorzów is one of the largest city parks in Europe.

q.q: Which historical region is Katowice part of?

Q2119.t: Streets with no names, laid out like a chessboard
Q2119.s: Mannheim's centre is a horseshoe of square blocks, and its streets have no names: addresses read like squares on a chessboard, such as Q6 or N1. The grid fills the angle where the Neckar flows into the Rhine. Across the Rhine, Ludwigshafen's enormous chemical works stretch along the bank, and on a clear night the two cities glow as one.
Q2119.w: A rounded grid of square blocks in the angle between the Rhine and the Neckar, with a vast chemical works across the Rhine.
f: In 1817 Karl Drais rode his two-wheeled 'running machine', an ancestor of the bicycle, out of Mannheim.
In 1888 Bertha Benz drove her husband's motor car from Mannheim to Pforzheim — the first long-distance car journey.
The BASF site in Ludwigshafen, across the Rhine, is one of the largest chemical complexes in the world.

q.q: What did Karl Drais ride out of Mannheim in 1817?

Q2256.t: Britain's canal city, far from any big river
Q2256.s: No great river runs through Birmingham, so in the 18th century the city dug its own waterways. Canals still thread between the red-brick districts, and locals like to claim the city has more of them than Venice. From cruise height, look instead for a knot of motorways on the north-eastern side: the tangle that earned the nickname Spaghetti Junction.
Q2256.w: A huge brick-red and green urban spread in the English Midlands; a knot of motorway loops on its north-eastern side.
f: The Gravelly Hill Interchange, better known as Spaghetti Junction, opened in 1972.
In the 18th century Matthew Boulton and James Watt built steam engines at their Soho works in Birmingham.
Birmingham is the most populous British city after London.

q.q: What is Birmingham's Gravelly Hill Interchange better known as?

Q18125.t: The first industrial city, at the foot of the Pennines
Q18125.s: The Pennine hills rise just east of Manchester, and their damp air and fast streams helped cotton turn it into the world's first industrial city. Look west for a dark ribbon heading towards the Mersey estuary: the Ship Canal. It was dug in the 1880s and 1890s so that ocean-going ships could sail right up to the city without stopping at Liverpool.
Q18125.w: A broad urban spread with the Pennine moors rising to the east; the Ship Canal runs west towards the Mersey estuary.
f: The Manchester Ship Canal, opened in 1894, is about 58 km long.
The Liverpool and Manchester Railway, opened in 1830, was the world's first inter-city passenger railway.
In 1948 the Manchester 'Baby' became the first computer to run a program stored in its own memory.

q.q: Which waterway lets ships sail from the Mersey estuary to Manchester?

Q2066.t: Coal country that has turned green
Q2066.s: This is where the Ruhr's chain of cities is at its densest, and yet much of what you see is green. Coal and steel built Essen; the pits have closed, leaving parks, woods and grassed-over spoil heaps. South of the centre, the river Ruhr widens into a long reservoir, the Baldeneysee, shining among wooded hills.
Q2066.w: A dense, green-flecked city in the Ruhr chain, with a long lake winding through wooded hills to the south.
f: The Zollverein colliery, once one of Europe's largest coal mines, has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2001.
Essen was named European Green Capital for 2017.
The Golden Madonna in Essen Cathedral, made around 980, is the oldest known fully sculpted figure of the Virgin Mary.

q.q: Which title did Essen hold in 2017?

Q495.t: An Alpine wall behind a Roman grid
Q495.s: Snowy Alps wrap around Turin in a great arc, often in plain sight from its streets. The city follows the Po, and its centre still keeps the rigid street grid of a Roman camp. Across the river rises a line of wooded hills. For four years, from 1861 to 1865, this was the capital of newly united Italy.
Q495.w: A large, regular city on the Po, with the Alps curving round to the west and north and green hills across the river.
f: Monviso (3,841 m), where the Po rises, stands about 65 km south-west of the city.
Fiat was founded in Turin in 1899.
Turin hosted the Winter Olympic Games in 2006.

q.q: Which car maker was founded in Turin in 1899?

Q39121.t: A wool town grown big in a Pennine valley
Q39121.s: Wool made Leeds rich: fleece from the Yorkshire hills was spun and woven in mills along the River Aire. The river and a canal still run side by side through the city, then head north-west into the Pennines. North of the centre, the land rolls up towards the Yorkshire Dales in green waves split by dry-stone walls.
Q39121.w: A large city in the Aire valley, with the river and canal running north-west towards the moors of the Pennines.
f: The Leeds and Liverpool Canal, about 204 km long, is the longest single canal in Britain.
Marks & Spencer began in 1884 as a penny stall in Leeds Kirkgate Market.
Louis Le Prince's Roundhay Garden Scene, filmed in Leeds in 1888, is the oldest surviving motion picture.

q.q: Which retailer began as a market stall in Leeds in 1884?

Q2044.t: A red-roofed bowl on the Arno
Q2044.s: Hills close in on three sides, and in the bowl between them lies a tight mass of terracotta roofs cut by the Arno. That is the Florence of the Renaissance, a centre small enough to cross on foot in half an hour. Around it Tuscany unrolls in olive groves, lines of cypress and vineyards; to the south lie the hills of Chianti.
Q2044.w: A compact reddish-brown city in a valley ringed by hills, with the Arno crossing it from east to west.
f: Brunelleschi's cathedral dome, completed in 1436, is still the largest brick dome ever built.
The gold florin, first struck here in 1252, became a standard coin of trade across medieval Europe.
The historic centre of Florence has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1982.

q.q: Which gold coin was first minted in Florence in 1252?

Q42308.t: A university city on the edge of the steppe
Q42308.s: Three small rivers, the Kharkiv, the Lopan and the Udy, meet within the city, and Kharkiv spreads out from their valleys across a plateau of black earth. Broad avenues and big green parks read clearly from the air. The city grew around a 17th-century fortress and became a centre of learning when its university opened in 1805.
Q42308.w: A large city on a flat plateau cut by shallow river valleys, surrounded by dark fields and patches of forest.
f: Kharkiv University, founded in 1805, is one of the oldest universities in the country.
Freedom Square, about 12 hectares, is one of the largest city squares in Europe.
The Derzhprom building, finished in 1928, was one of the first Soviet skyscrapers.

q.q: In which year did Kharkiv University open?

Q36600.t: The Dutch seat of power that isn't the capital
Q36600.s: Parliament, the government and the king's working palace are all here, yet The Hague is not the Dutch capital; that title belongs to Amsterdam. The city runs straight into a line of pale dunes and the North Sea at Scheveningen. To the south-west, look for acres of glinting glass: the greenhouses of the Westland, one of the most intensively farmed corners of Europe.
Q36600.w: A city pressed against pale coastal dunes, with the shining glasshouses of the Westland spreading to the south-west.
f: The Peace Palace, opened in 1913, houses the International Court of Justice.
Scheveningen, the city's seaside district, grew from a fishing village and has a pier over the North Sea.
The city's formal Dutch name, 's-Gravenhage, means 'the Count's hedge'.

q.q: Which UN court sits in The Hague?
x: The European Court of Human Rights

Q23482.t: France's oldest city, framed by white cliffs
Q23482.s: Blinding white limestone hems Marseille in: bare hills behind, and to the south-east the Calanques, narrow fjord-like inlets cut into cliffs above turquoise water. Offshore lie the pale, treeless Frioul islands. Greek sailors from Phocaea founded a trading post here around 600 BC, which is why Marseille is called the oldest city in France.
Q23482.w: A large pale city around a bay, with white limestone hills behind, bare islands offshore and cliffs to the south-east.
f: The Calanques became a national park in 2012, reaching right to the edge of the city.
The Château d'If, on a small island offshore, is the prison of 'The Count of Monte Cristo'.
Marseille-Fos is the largest port in France.

q.q: Greek settlers from which city founded Marseille?

Q36433.t: Steep banks and bridges over the Douro
Q36433.s: The Douro runs its last few kilometres in a deep gorge, with Porto piled up on the north bank and Vila Nova de Gaia facing it from the south. Six bridges stitch the two together. Boats once brought port wine down from vineyard terraces far upriver, and the lodges where it matures still line the Gaia shore. Beyond, Atlantic surf draws a white line.
Q36433.w: A city on steep banks where the Douro gorge meets the Atlantic, the river crossed by a string of bridges.
f: Portugal takes its name from Portus Cale, the Roman-era settlement at the mouth of the Douro.
The two-deck Dom Luís I bridge, finished in 1886, was designed by Théophile Seyrig, a former partner of Gustave Eiffel.
Porto's historic centre has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1996.

q.q: Which river meets the Atlantic at Porto?

Q42448.t: Steel city with one foot in the Peak District
Q42448.s: Where the houses stop, the moors begin. Sheffield climbs over steep hills where five rivers meet, and its western edge runs straight into the Peak District; a sizeable slice of the city lies inside the national park. Fast streams once turned the grinding wheels of the cutlers here, and the city's name became a byword for steel.
Q42448.w: A hilly city in green valleys, its western edge meeting the brown moorland of the Peak District.
f: Harry Brearley developed stainless steel in Sheffield in 1913.
Sheffield FC, founded in 1857, is recognised as the world's oldest football club.
The city takes its name from the River Sheaf, one of the five rivers that meet here.

q.q: Which material did Harry Brearley develop in Sheffield in 1913?

Q2100.t: A sea of docks where the Ruhr meets the Rhine
Q2100.s: Harbour basins, rail yards and container stacks lace the water where the Ruhr flows into the Rhine. This is Duisport, often called the largest inland port in the world, and barges from the North Sea ports come up the Rhine to unload here. North of the city, an old ironworks has been kept as a park and is lit up in colour after dark.
Q2100.w: Long, finger-like harbour basins on the Rhine at the mouth of the Ruhr, with industry and rail lines around them.
f: The cartographer Gerardus Mercator lived and worked in Duisburg for more than 40 years.
Landschaftspark Duisburg-Nord turned an ironworks, closed in 1985, into a public park.
The Rhine at Duisburg is a busy barge highway linking the Ruhr with Rotterdam and the North Sea.

q.q: Which famous mapmaker lived and worked in Duisburg?

Q1718.t: The village on the Düssel that grew rich on the Rhine
Q1718.s: The Rhine swings through Düsseldorf in wide loops, with the old town on the east bank and broad green meadows along the water. The name means 'village on the Düssel', after a small stream that joins the big river here. Today the capital of North Rhine-Westphalia is a city of fashion, advertising and art.
Q1718.w: Wide meanders of the Rhine with the city mostly on the east bank; the airport lies just to the north.
f: The poet Heinrich Heine was born in Düsseldorf in 1797.
Düsseldorf is home to one of the largest Japanese communities in Europe.
The Königsallee, a shopping boulevard, runs along both sides of an old moat.

q.q: What does 'Dorf' mean in the name Düsseldorf?

Q898.t: A fortress city where the Om meets the Irtysh
Q898.s: Across the flat West Siberian plain the Irtysh loops broad and brown, and at the point where the little Om joins it, Omsk spreads over both banks. It began in 1716 as a wooden fortress on Russia's southern frontier. Beyond the last suburbs the land is almost perfectly level: birch groves, fields and lakes stretching away in every direction.
Q898.w: A large city on a sweeping bend of the Irtysh where a smaller river joins from the east, in flat farmland.
f: Dostoevsky served four years of penal labour in Omsk, later retold in 'Notes from the House of the Dead'.
The Trans-Siberian Railway crosses the Irtysh at Omsk.
The Om, which gives the city its name, flows for more than 1,000 km before joining the Irtysh.

q.q: Which river does the Om flow into at Omsk?

Q906.t: An industrial giant among the lakes of the Urals
Q906.s: Lakes are scattered around Chelyabinsk like dropped coins, catching the light where the Urals flatten into the West Siberian plain. Several reach right up to the city's edge. Founded in 1736 as a fortress on the Miass river, the city grew into a giant of steel and tractor building after the railway arrived.
Q906.w: A large grey city on flat land peppered with round lakes, with low wooded Ural ridges to the west.
f: Chelyabinsk was founded in 1736 as a fortress on the Miass river.
In 1892 the West Siberian section of the Trans-Siberian Railway began to be built eastwards from Chelyabinsk.
Lake Smolino, inside the city limits, is a salt lake.

q.q: On which river was Chelyabinsk founded?

Q908.t: Gateway to the Caucasus on the lower Don
Q908.s: The Don makes its final run to the Sea of Azov here, broad and slow, and Rostov lines its high right bank. Across the river lie low meadows and reed beds, and a little downstream the Don begins to split into the channels of its delta. The city grew from a customs post set up in 1749, and grain and river trade made it rich.
Q908.w: A big city on the high north bank of the Don, facing flat green floodplain, with the river's delta to the west.
f: Rostov began in 1749 as the Temernik customs post, set up by decree of Empress Elizabeth.
Nakhichevan-on-Don, founded by Armenian settlers from Crimea in 1779, is now part of the city.
The Sea of Azov, fed by the Don, is the shallowest sea in the world, nowhere much deeper than 14 m.

q.q: What was Rostov-on-Don founded as in 1749?

Q48256.t: A long city on a river as wide as a lake
Q48256.s: The Dnieper is so broad here that it looks more like a lake than a river, with islands in mid-stream and bridges strung between the banks. Dnipro stretches for kilometres along the water. It was founded in the late 18th century as Yekaterinoslav, 'the glory of Catherine', in honour of Catherine the Great, and grew into a city of steel and rocket-building.
Q48256.w: A long city on both banks of a very wide Dnieper, with wooded islands in mid-river and several bridges.
f: Just downstream the river once tumbled over the Dnieper Rapids; since the 1930s they have lain under a reservoir.
The Dnieper, about 2,200 km long, is the fourth-longest river in Europe.
Space launchers such as the Zenit and the Cyclone were designed in Dnipro.

q.q: What was Dnipro called when it was founded?

Q648.t: Flemish brick and a star-shaped citadel
Q648.s: Flat Flanders stretches in every direction, and Lille's brick-red sprawl runs on without a break into Roubaix and Tourcoing, right up to the Belgian border. Look for a green five-pointed shape north-west of the centre: the citadel that Vauban built after 1667, still ringed by water. High-speed trains now put Lille about an hour from Paris and within easy reach of London and Brussels.
Q648.w: A reddish urban mass on flat farmland merging into neighbouring towns to the north-east; a green pentagon marks the citadel.
f: Vauban's citadel in Lille is nicknamed the 'Queen of Citadels'.
Charles de Gaulle was born in Lille in 1890.
The Braderie de Lille, held each September, is one of Europe's largest flea markets.

q.q: Which French leader was born in Lille in 1890?

Q34370.t: Europe's biggest port, reaching out to sea
Q34370.s: Follow the Maas from Rotterdam towards the sea and you trace Europe's largest port: some 40 km of docks, tank farms and container stacks. At its far end the port has pushed out into the North Sea on land built from sand. The city itself, with its skyline of towers and bridges, sits among flat green polders cut by straight canals.
Q34370.w: A long band of docks and pale storage tanks running west to the North Sea, with the city at its inland end.
f: The port of Rotterdam is the largest in Europe.
Maasvlakte 2, a port extension on land reclaimed from the North Sea, opened in 2013.
The Renaissance scholar Erasmus was born in Rotterdam in the 1460s.

q.q: Which river branch flows through the centre of Rotterdam?

Q365.t: A Roman city in a half-circle on the Rhine
Q365.s: Cologne draws a half-moon on the west bank of the Rhine: its old centre is ringed by boulevards that follow the line of the medieval walls, with the river as the straight edge. The Romans made it a colony in AD 50, and the name Cologne comes from the Latin colonia. Across the river, the Deutz district faces the old town.
Q365.w: A semicircular city on the west bank of the Rhine, its centre outlined by a ring of boulevards.
f: Cologne Cathedral's twin spires reach 157 m; from 1880 to 1884 it was the tallest building in the world.
Eau de Cologne was first made here in the early 18th century by the Italian perfumer Johann Maria Farina.
The city's Roman name was Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium.

q.q: What record did Cologne Cathedral hold from 1880 to 1884?

Q1874.t: A grid of streets on a Black Sea bluff
Q1874.s: A neat grid of streets on a high bluff above the Black Sea: from the air, Odessa's centre looks drawn with a ruler. North and south-west of the city, long salty lagoons called limans reach inland like fingers. The city was founded in 1794 and grew quickly as a free port shipping grain from the steppe.
Q1874.w: A gridded city on a coastal bluff with harbour moles, and long narrow lagoons reaching inland on either side.
f: Odessa was founded in 1794 on the orders of Catherine the Great.
Beneath the city lie the Odessa Catacombs, old limestone quarries often said to total some 2,500 km.
The Potemkin Stairs, leading down to the port, have 192 steps.

q.q: In which year was Odessa founded?

Q43070.t: Pyramids of coal waste on the open steppe
Q43070.s: Scattered across the steppe around Donetsk stand dark cones, some as tall as small hills. They are spoil heaps from more than a century of coal mining in the Donbas, the Donets coal basin. The city grew from a works settlement founded in 1869 by the Welsh industrialist John Hughes, and its first name, Yuzovka, came from his surname.
Q43070.w: A large city on open steppe, with dark conical spoil heaps, ponds and industrial sites scattered around it.
f: The name Donbas is short for 'Donets Basin', after the Siverskyi Donets river to the north.
Donetsk is known for its parks and rose gardens.
The Kalmius river runs through the city on its way south to the Sea of Azov.

q.q: Where did John Hughes, founder of Donetsk's ironworks, come from?

Q8692.t: An iron town reborn in a green Basque valley
Q8692.s: Steep green hills crowd in on Bilbao, leaving room only for the winding estuary of the Nervión and the city strung along it. Ships and iron made the city rich; the river then leads about 15 km to the open Bay of Biscay. In 1997 a titanium-clad art museum by Frank Gehry gave the old port a new face and a new name abroad.
Q8692.w: A city squeezed into a narrow, winding estuary between green hills, opening out north-west to the Bay of Biscay.
f: The Vizcaya Bridge near the estuary mouth, opened in 1893, is the world's oldest transporter bridge.
Bilbao was founded as a town in 1300.
The Guggenheim Museum Bilbao, designed by Frank Gehry, opened in 1997.

q.q: What kind of bridge crosses the estuary mouth near Bilbao?

Q3426.t: Where Peter the Great built his first fleet
Q3426.s: A long, narrow reservoir runs right through Voronezh, splitting it into two banks joined by bridges; locals call it the Voronezh sea. Around the city lies some of Russia's blackest, richest soil. In the 1690s Peter the Great built shipyards on the river here, and the ships launched from them became the first Russian navy.
Q3426.w: A big city split by a long, narrow reservoir running north–south, with dark farmland all around.
f: The Voronezh reservoir is about 30 km long.
Russia's first naval squadron was built in Voronezh in 1695–1696 for Peter the Great's campaign against Azov.
A replica of Peter's ship of the line Goto Predestination, launched here in 1700, is moored in the city.

q.q: Which ruler built a fleet at Voronezh in the 1690s?

Q5332.t: Two cities facing each other across the Volga
Q5332.s: The Volga here spreads kilometres wide, with Saratov climbing the hills of the right bank and Engels spread out on the flat left bank opposite. A bridge nearly 3 km long ties them together. Wooded hills close in on the city from the west. A young Yuri Gagarin learned to fly at the Saratov aero club in the 1950s.
Q5332.w: A very wide stretch of the Volga with a big city on the hilly west bank and another on the flat east bank.
f: The Saratov road bridge over the Volga, opened in 1965, is about 2.8 km long.
Yuri Gagarin landed near Engels, across the Volga from Saratov, after the first human spaceflight.
The Saratov accordion is known for the little bells fitted to its body.

q.q: Who landed near Saratov after the first human spaceflight?

Q36036.t: Rain here can end up in two different seas
Q36036.s: Rain falling on Lviv can end up in two different seas. The city sits on the main European watershed: streams on one side drain towards the Baltic, those on the other to the Black Sea. Its medieval centre is ringed by green hills, and even its own river, the Poltva, is out of sight, running in a tunnel beneath the streets.
Q36036.w: A compact city among green hills and patches of forest, surrounded by rolling farmland.
f: Lviv was founded in the mid-13th century and named after Prince Lev, son of King Danylo of Galicia.
The historic centre of Lviv has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1998.
The Poltva river, hidden under the centre, eventually drains to the Baltic via the Bug and the Vistula.

q.q: After whom was Lviv named?

Q1479.t: A moon-shaped bend of the Garonne among vineyards
Q1479.s: The Garonne curves through Bordeaux in a perfect crescent, which is why the old harbour is called the Port of the Moon. Around the city the land is striped with vineyards, among the most famous in the world. A little way downstream the Garonne joins the Dordogne to form the Gironde, a wide brown estuary running out to the Atlantic.
Q1479.w: A crescent-shaped bend of the river with the city on its inner bank; vineyards and the broad Gironde estuary to the north.
f: The Port of the Moon, the crescent-shaped historic city, became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2007.
The Gironde is the largest estuary in Western Europe.
The Dune of Pilat, the tallest sand dune in Europe at over 100 m, lies about 60 km to the south-west.

q.q: Which two rivers meet below Bordeaux to form the Gironde?

Q31487.t: A royal city in a bend of the Vistula
Q31487.s: The Vistula swings round Wawel Hill, where Polish kings were crowned and buried, and the medieval town fans out to the north. A ring of park, the Planty, now follows the line of the old walls. On clear days the jagged Tatras show on the southern horizon. Kraków was Poland's capital until the royal court moved to Warsaw at the end of the 16th century.
Q31487.w: A large city on a loop of the Vistula, with a big steelworks to the east and hills rising towards the south.
f: Kraków's old town was among the first sites put on UNESCO's World Heritage List, in 1978.
The Wieliczka Salt Mine, just south-east of the city, was worked from the 13th century to the late 20th.
The Planty park, about 4 km long, rings the old town where medieval walls once stood.

q.q: Which river flows past Wawel Hill in Kraków?

Q1792.t: Amber, grain and a sand spit across the bay
Q1792.s: A thin arm of sand curls across Gdańsk Bay: the Hel Peninsula, some 35 km long and in places only a few hundred metres wide. Gdańsk sits at the bottom of the bay, joined to Sopot and Gdynia in one long coastal city. For centuries grain floated down the Vistula to this Hanseatic port, and amber washed up on its beaches.
Q1792.w: A city at the head of a wide bay, a long thin sand spit curving across it, the flat Vistula delta to the east.
f: Sopot's wooden pier, just north of Gdańsk, is about 500 m long — the longest wooden pier in Europe.
The Vistula, Poland's longest river, reaches the Baltic just east of the city.
Baltic amber is still worked in Gdańsk, which calls itself the world capital of amber.

q.q: Which trading league was Gdańsk a leading member of?

Q1903.t: Built of black lava at the foot of Etna
Q1903.s: Etna fills the view to the north: a vast dark mountain, often trailing a plume of steam and snow-capped in winter. Catania spreads along the coast at its foot, and much of the old city is built from the volcano's own dark lava stone. South of the city, the flat Plain of Catania opens out, a patchwork of citrus groves and fields.
Q1903.w: A coastal city beneath a huge, dark volcanic cone to the north, with a broad flat plain opening to the south.
f: Etna rises to more than 3,300 m, about 30 km from the city centre, and is one of the most active volcanoes on Earth.
Mount Etna became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2013.
The composer Vincenzo Bellini was born in Catania in 1801.

q.q: Which composer was born in Catania in 1801?

Q3646.t: Cossack city on the looping Kuban
Q3646.s: The Kuban wanders across the flat plain in great loops and cut-off oxbows, and Krasnodar grew on its northern bank. Just upstream, a large reservoir shines on the plain. All around lie some of Russia's most fertile fields, and downstream, towards the Sea of Azov, many of them are flooded paddies: this is Russia's main rice-growing region.
Q3646.w: A large city on a meandering river, with a big reservoir just to the east and a chequerboard of fields all around.
f: Black Sea Cossacks founded the city in 1793 as Yekaterinodar, 'Catherine's gift'.
The Krasnodar reservoir on the Kuban is the largest reservoir in the North Caucasus.
The Kuban flows about 870 km from the glaciers of Elbrus to the Sea of Azov.

q.q: What was Krasnodar called until 1920?

Q5627.t: A high bank above Europe's largest reservoir
Q5627.s: No longer a river but a broad inland sea: that is the Volga at Ulyanovsk, part of the Kuybyshev reservoir. The old town sits high on the steep right bank, with newer districts across the water on the flat left bank, joined by long bridges. The city was founded in 1648 as the fortress of Simbirsk; its present name honours Lenin, born here in 1870.
Q5627.w: A city on both sides of a very wide stretch of the Volga, linked by long bridges, the old town on the higher west bank.
f: The Kuybyshev reservoir on the Volga is the largest reservoir in Europe.
Ivan Goncharov, author of 'Oblomov', was born in Simbirsk in 1812.
The city was renamed Ulyanovsk in 1924, after Lenin's family name, Ulyanov.

q.q: What was Ulyanovsk called until 1924?

Q1731.t: Florence on the Elbe, framed by green meadows
Q1731.s: The Elbe curves gently through Dresden between wide green meadows that have been left unbuilt, so the river keeps its countryside look right in the city centre. The baroque old town rises on the south bank. Upstream to the south-east, the river heads into Saxon Switzerland, a maze of sandstone towers and deep gorges.
Q1731.w: A city along a gently curving river bordered by broad green meadows, with wooded hills to the north-east.
f: Its baroque skyline earned Dresden the nickname 'Florence on the Elbe'.
European hard-paste porcelain was first made in Dresden in 1708; production moved to nearby Meissen in 1710.
The sandstone towers of Saxon Switzerland begin about 30 km upstream.

q.q: What nickname did its baroque skyline earn Dresden?

Q2423.t: A thousand-year-old city where two rivers meet
Q2423.s: Look for the point where the Kotorosl flows into the Volga: that spit of land, the Strelka, is where Yaroslavl began. According to tradition, Prince Yaroslav the Wise founded the city around 1010. Its old centre, with streets fanning out from the riverfront, is one of the jewels of the Golden Ring of old Russian towns.
Q2423.w: A big city on the Volga, with a smaller river joining from the south-west near the centre.
f: The historic centre of Yaroslavl has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2005.
Valentina Tereshkova, the first woman in space, was born in a village near Yaroslavl in 1937.
The city's coat of arms shows a bear carrying an axe.

q.q: Which animal appears on Yaroslavl's coat of arms?

Q4454.t: The city on the banknote, where the Amur is vast
Q4454.s: A maze of channels, islands and sandbanks kilometres wide: that is the Amur at Khabarovsk, joined by the Ussuri just upstream. The city lines the high right bank. A long bridge carrying both a road and a railway spans the river. The city began in 1858 as a military post and took its name from the 17th-century explorer Yerofey Khabarov.
Q4454.w: A long city on the high east bank of a huge braided river, with a long bridge across it and flat wetlands beyond.
f: Khabarovsk and its Amur bridge appear on the Russian 5,000-rouble banknote.
The Ussuri joins the Amur just south-west of the city.
In winter the Amur freezes hard enough for people to walk far out onto the ice.

q.q: Which explorer is Khabarovsk named after?

Q5337.t: A steppe city on the river between two continents
Q5337.s: Open steppe runs to the horizon, and through it the Ural river winds in tight loops, lined by a green ribbon of floodplain woods. Orenburg stands on the high bank above. The river is often taken as a boundary between Europe and Asia, and a footbridge in the city lets you walk from one to the other. Gas fields spread across the plain to the south.
Q5337.w: A city on a high riverbank above a meandering, tree-lined river, with flat yellow-brown steppe all around.
f: Orenburg's gossamer down shawls are said to be fine enough to pull through a wedding ring.
Yuri Gagarin trained at the military flight school in Orenburg and married a local girl here in 1957.
The Orenburg gas field, one of the largest in Europe, lies just south of the city.

q.q: What is Orenburg famous for making?

Q93910.t: Steel smoke in a valley of the Kuzbass
Q93910.s: Mountains close in around Novokuznetsk: the Kuznetsk Alatau to the east, the dark taiga of Mountain Shoria to the south. The city follows the Tom along the valley floor, with vast steelworks on its edges and coal pits scarring the hills. It began in 1618 as the Kuznetsk fortress, named after the local people's skill as blacksmiths.
Q93910.w: An industrial city strung along a river valley, with steelworks, coal pits and forested mountains to the east and south.
f: Sheregesh, one of Siberia's best-known ski resorts, lies in the mountains of Mountain Shoria to the south.
Fyodor Dostoevsky married Maria Isaeva in Kuznetsk in 1857.
Novokuznetsk is one of the main steel-making centres of Siberia.

q.q: Which writer married in Kuznetsk, now Novokuznetsk, in 1857?

Q2746.t: A kremlin above the Oka's flooding meadows
Q2746.s: The Oka swings past Ryazan in wide loops, and across the river a sea of flat meadows and forest stretches north towards the lakes and marshes of Meshchera. The city climbs the higher southern bank, where the kremlin stands on a hill above two small streams. In late spring the Oka floods its meadows for kilometres, turning them into a shining lake.
Q2746.w: A city on the south bank of a looping river, facing a broad green floodplain and dark forests to the north.
f: Ivan Pavlov, the first Russian Nobel laureate, was born in Ryazan in 1849.
The poet Sergei Yesenin was born in 1895 in Konstantinovo, a village on the Oka in the Ryazan region.
Until 1778 the city was called Pereyaslavl-Ryazansky.

q.q: Which Nobel-winning scientist was born in Ryazan?

Q5815.t: Siberia's first Russian town, now an oil capital
Q5815.s: Tyumen was the first foothold: founded in 1586 on the Tura, it is considered the oldest Russian town in Siberia. From the air the city is ringed by pine and birch forest, with bogs and lakes glinting beyond. Today it runs the oil and gas fields far to the north, and its hot springs let people bathe outdoors in the depths of winter.
Q5815.w: A large city on a winding river in flat forest land, with lakes and bogs scattered around it.
f: The Trans-Siberian Railway runs through Tyumen on its way from the Urals to Omsk.
Warm water from deep thermal springs around Tyumen fills outdoor pools that stay open all winter.
The Tura, on which the city stands, flows into the Tobol, a tributary of the Irtysh.

q.q: In which year was Tyumen founded?

Q5540.t: A frontier fortress where forest meets steppe
Q5540.s: Penza marks the meeting of forest and steppe: patches of woodland give way to wide fields, and the city spreads along the Sura in between. It was founded in 1663 as a fortress guarding Russia's south-eastern frontier. South-west of the city a large reservoir fills the Sura valley. The poet Lermontov grew up on an estate in this region.
Q5540.w: A city on a small river among fields and patches of forest, with a long reservoir to the south-west.
f: Penza was founded in 1663 as a fortress on the Sura.
Mikhail Lermontov grew up at Tarkhany, his grandmother's estate in the Penza region, where he is buried.
The Sura, which flows through the city, is a tributary of the Volga.

q.q: Which poet grew up at Tarkhany in the Penza region?

Q3927.t: Where the Volga shatters into a maze of channels
Q3927.s: South of Astrakhan the Volga falls apart: hundreds of channels, reed beds and islands fan out towards the Caspian Sea in the largest river delta in Europe. The city itself stands on islands in the upper delta, around a white-walled 16th-century kremlin. In summer, whole bays of the lower delta turn pink with blooming lotus.
Q3927.w: A city among river channels at the head of a vast delta of reed beds and waterways spreading south-east to the Caspian.
f: The Volga delta, which begins just upstream of Astrakhan, is the largest river delta in Europe.
Astrakhan's kremlin was built of stone in the late 16th century.
The curly lamb fur called astrakhan takes its name from the city.

q.q: Which river's delta begins near Astrakhan?

Q384.t: Strung along the Vardar beneath a steep mountain
Q384.s: Mountains frame Skopje on every side, and the city stretches for kilometres along the Vardar on the floor of the basin. Mount Vodno rises steeply right above its southern edge. A little to the south-west, the Treska river cuts the deep Matka canyon, now a narrow reservoir. In the old bazaar across the Stone Bridge, streets keep an Ottoman pattern.
Q384.w: A long city on a river in a mountain-ringed basin, with a steep wooded peak rising right above its southern edge.
f: Mother Teresa was born in Skopje in 1910.
The Stone Bridge over the Vardar was built in the 15th century.
Matka Canyon, with its caves and small reservoir, lies about 15 km south-west of the centre.

q.q: Which river flows through Skopje?

Q6066.s: The Tom cuts through Kemerovo in a broad curve, with the city on both banks and dark taiga beyond. Around it the land is stripped in places by open-pit coal mines, terraced like giant steps. This is the Kuzbass, one of the world's great coalfields, and the story of its coal began on this riverbank three centuries ago.
Q6066.w: A city on both banks of a curving river, with grey terraced open-pit mines and dark forest around it.
f: In 1721 the ore prospector Mikhail Volkov found coal on the Tom here — the first recorded find in the Kuzbass.
The city grew from the villages of Shcheglovo and Kemerovo and took its present name in 1932.
The Kuznetsk Basin, or Kuzbass, is one of the largest coalfields in the world.

q.q: In which year was coal first found at Kemerovo?

Q25270.t: A hill city where the Kosovo plain begins
Q25270.s: Pristina climbs over low hills where the flat Kosovo plain meets forested uplands to the east. Around 650 m above sea level, the city is the largest in Kosovo. West of it, look for grey open-pit mines and the smokestacks of power stations: the area sits on some of the largest lignite deposits in Europe. Wooded Germia Park reaches into the city from the east.
Q25270.w: A city on low hills with a broad plain to the west, grey open-pit mines beyond, and wooded uplands to the east.
f: The Kosovo plain west of the city is drained by the Sitnica river, which flows north.
The ruins of Ulpiana, a Roman city, lie about 10 km to the south-east.
Germia Park, the forested hills on the city's eastern edge, is Pristina's largest green space.

q.q: Which ancient Roman city's ruins lie just south-east of Pristina?

Q5384.t: A river-bend city of clay toys and taiga
Q5384.s: The Vyatka loops lazily through a green sea of forest, and Kirov stands on the high bank of one of its great bends. The city has worn three names: Khlynov, Vyatka and, since 1934, Kirov. Across the river lies the village of Dymkovo, where craftswomen have long shaped and painted bright clay toys, one of Russia's best-known folk crafts.
Q5384.w: A city on a high bank inside a big loop of a river, with endless taiga around it.
f: Dymkovo toys — clay figures whitewashed and painted in bright patterns — are named after a village across the river.
The city's founding is traditionally dated to 1374.
The Vyatka flows for more than 1,300 km before joining the Kama.

q.q: What are Dymkovo toys, made near Kirov, made of?

Q10686.t: A shipbuilding city at the head of a sea lough
Q10686.s: Belfast Lough runs inland like a long funnel, and the city fills its head, where the river Lagan comes in. Dark hills rise steeply on the north-western side: Cave Hill's cliffs are said to resemble Napoleon's profile. Shipbuilding made the city famous, and two huge yellow gantry cranes still stand over the docks. Just west glints Lough Neagh.
Q10686.w: A city at the end of a funnel-shaped sea inlet, with steep dark hills to the north-west and a huge lake further west.
f: Lough Neagh, about 25 km west of the city, is the largest lake in the British Isles.
The shipyard's yellow gantry cranes, Samson and Goliath, are each about 100 m tall.
Queen's University Belfast was founded in 1845.

q.q: Which is the largest lake in the British Isles, just west of Belfast?

Q1829.t: Königsberg's bridges, amber and sand spits
Q1829.s: Look for the Pregolya river winding into a shallow lagoon, and beyond it two impossibly thin sand spits running along the Baltic coast: the Vistula Spit to the south-west and the Curonian Spit to the north-east. Kaliningrad sits between them. Until 1946 it was Königsberg, the city of the philosopher Kant, and its bridges gave rise to a famous puzzle.
Q1829.w: A city on a river flowing into a lagoon, with long, pencil-thin sand spits along the sea coast to the south-west and north-east.
f: In 1736 Leonhard Euler proved that no walk could cross Königsberg's seven bridges exactly once each, founding graph theory.
The philosopher Immanuel Kant was born in Königsberg in 1724 and lived there almost all his life.
The Curonian Spit, about 98 km long, has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2000.

q.q: Which mathematician solved the Seven Bridges of Königsberg puzzle?

Q2801.t: A city named after the thickets of the Desna
Q2801.s: Deep forests have always surrounded Bryansk, and its name is thought to come from the old Russian word for dense thickets. The city spreads across both banks of the Desna, broken up by steep, wooded ravines. The river wanders across a wide green floodplain, and beyond it the woods run on to the south for many kilometres.
Q2801.w: A city on both sides of a winding river, cut by ravines and surrounded by broad forests.
f: Bryansk was first mentioned in a chronicle in 1146.
The poet Fyodor Tyutchev was born in 1803 at Ovstug, a family estate in the Bryansk region.
The Desna, which flows through the city, is a large tributary of the Dnieper.

q.q: Which poet was born at Ovstug near Bryansk in 1803?

Q1780.t: A capital on the Danube that touches two borders
Q1780.s: Austria and Hungary both begin at the city limits: Bratislava is the only capital that borders two other countries. The Danube divides it, with the castle hill and old town on the north bank and the vast high-rise estate of Petržalka across the water. The Little Carpathians start right in the city, their slopes striped with vineyards running away to the north-east.
Q1780.w: A city on both banks of the Danube, with wooded hills rising to the north and flat farmland to the south.
f: Vienna and Bratislava are about 55 km apart, the closest pair of capitals in Europe after Rome and Vatican City.
Hungarian kings and queens were crowned in Bratislava's St Martin's Cathedral from 1563 to 1830.
Petržalka, on the south bank, is one of the largest housing estates in Central Europe.

q.q: Which two countries border Bratislava?

Q95449.t: A steel giant built beside a mountain of iron
Q95449.s: Magnitogorsk was built from scratch from 1929 beside Magnitnaya, a mountain so rich in magnetic iron ore that it has now been largely dug away. The steelworks stretches for kilometres along a reservoir on the Ural river. Because the river runs through the city, Magnitogorsk lies partly in Europe and partly in Asia.
Q95449.w: A huge steelworks along a long reservoir on a river, with the city on both sides and open steppe beyond.
f: Construction of the city and its steelworks began in 1929 on the open steppe.
The Magnitogorsk steelworks is one of the largest in Russia.

q.q: What gave Magnitogorsk its name?

Q2288.t: A Volga city halfway between two capitals
Q2288.s: Halfway between Moscow and St Petersburg, the railway and main road linking the two cities cut straight through Tver. The Volga, still young here, crosses the city in a gentle curve and is joined by the Tvertsa and the Tmaka. From Tver in the 15th century, a merchant named Afanasy Nikitin set off on a journey that took him all the way to India.
Q2288.w: A city on both banks of a medium-sized river, with a straight railway and motorway running north-west to south-east.
f: Afanasy Nikitin described his journey to India in 'A Journey Beyond Three Seas'.
The Volga's source in the Valdai Hills is only a few hundred kilometres upstream.
In the 14th century Tver was a powerful principality and a rival of Moscow.

q.q: Which Tver merchant travelled to India in the 15th century?

Q98967.t: Where the Demidovs forged iron for Europe
Q98967.s: Nizhny Tagil sprawls between forested Ural ridges, around a long dammed pond that once drove the ironworks' waterwheels. The Demidov family founded the works in the 1720s, and the town grew into one of the great iron centres of the Russian Empire. Look for the huge terraced pit on the edge of town: Mount Vysokaya, a hill of iron ore mined into a hole.
Q98967.w: An industrial city around a long pond, with deep terraced mining pits and forested Ural ridges around it.
f: In 1834 the Cherepanovs, father and son, built Russia's first steam locomotive here.
Demidov iron, stamped with a sable, was prized in 18th-century England as 'Old Sable'.
The Nizhny Tagil Charter of 2003, the international charter for industrial heritage, is named after the city.

q.q: What did the Cherepanovs build in Nizhny Tagil in 1834?

Q8745.t: A deep Atlantic inlet dotted with mussel rafts
Q8745.s: The Ría de Vigo reaches deep into the green Galician hills, and at its mouth the granite Cíes Islands stand guard against the Atlantic. Look closely at the calm water: it is freckled with hundreds of small dark squares, rafts where mussels are grown on hanging ropes. Vigo climbs the southern shore, one of Europe's busiest fishing ports.
Q8745.w: A long sea inlet between green hills, with rocky islands at its mouth and rows of tiny rafts on the water.
f: The Cíes Islands are part of the Atlantic Islands of Galicia National Park.
The Rande Bridge spans the ría at its narrowest point, upstream of the city.
Galicia's rías produce most of Spain's mussels, grown on thousands of floating rafts.

q.q: Which islands guard the mouth of the Ría de Vigo?

Q11974.t: Beach on one side, port on the other, sand between
Q11974.s: At the north-eastern tip of Gran Canaria, a volcanic knob called La Isleta is tied to the island by a narrow sandy isthmus. Las Palmas fills that neck, with a long beach on one side and a busy port on the other, then runs south along the coast. Behind it, bare ravines climb towards the island's volcanic heights.
Q11974.w: A city on the north-east corner of a round island, stretched along the coast and spreading onto a rocky peninsula.
f: Las Palmas was founded in 1478.
Columbus stopped at Gran Canaria in 1492 on his first voyage across the Atlantic.
Las Canteras beach is sheltered by a natural offshore reef called La Barra.

q.q: In which year was Las Palmas founded?

Q5206.t: The 'city of the cross' on a high plateau
Q5206.s: Stavropol has a head start on height: it sprawls over the Stavropol Upland, with woods on its slopes and the steppe spreading out far below. It was founded in 1777 as one of a chain of fortresses guarding the empire's new southern frontier, and its Greek name means 'city of the cross'. On a clear day the snowy Caucasus may show far to the south.
Q5206.w: A large city on a raised, partly wooded plateau, with a patchwork of farmland spreading away in every direction.
f: Stavropol was founded in 1777 as a fortress on the Azov–Mozdok defensive line.
The city is the capital of Stavropol Krai, one of southern Russia's main grain-growing regions.

q.q: What does the name Stavropol mean?

Q6816.t: Where the Trans-Siberian turns off for Mongolia
Q6816.s: Bare steppe hills and dark forested ridges meet around Ulan-Ude, where the little Uda flows into the broad, braided Selenga. The name means 'Red Uda'. Lake Baikal lies less than 100 km to the north-west, and the Mongolian border about 200 km to the south. This is the heart of Buryatia, where Buddhist monasteries stand among the hills.
Q6816.w: A city where two rivers meet in a broad valley, with bare steppe hills and forested ridges around.
f: Just outside the city the Trans-Mongolian Railway branches off the Trans-Siberian towards Ulaanbaatar and Beijing.
The Ivolginsky datsan, south-west of the city, is a leading centre of Buddhism in Russia.
A bronze head of Lenin about 7.7 m tall, one of the largest ever made, stands in the main square.

q.q: What does the name Ulan-Ude mean?

Q39420.t: A subtropical coast under snowy peaks
Q39420.s: Palm trees on the beach and snow on the peaks: Sochi squeezes a thin ribbon of subtropical coast between the Black Sea and the forested slopes of the Caucasus. Greater Sochi runs for about 145 km along the shore. Up in the mountains to the east lies Krasnaya Polyana, where the ski and sledding events of the 2014 Winter Olympics were held.
Q39420.w: A long, thin strip of town along the sea, backed by steep green mountains with snowy summits behind.
f: Greater Sochi stretches about 145 km along the Black Sea coast.
Sochi hosted the Winter Olympic Games in 2014.
Tea has grown on the hills around Sochi since the early 20th century, in some of the world's most northerly tea gardens.

q.q: In which year did Sochi host the Winter Olympics?

Q46852.t: The old Moldavian capital on seven hills
Q46852.s: Like Rome, Iași is said to stand on seven hills, rolling above the valley of the little Bahlui. For three centuries this was the capital of the Principality of Moldavia, and it remains a city of churches, theatres and students. East of the city, the land drops to the wide green floodplain of the Prut.
Q46852.w: A city spread over low hills above a small river valley, with a wide green floodplain to the east.
f: Iași was the capital of Moldavia from 1564 to 1859.
Romania's first modern university was founded in Iași in 1860.
The Prut river flows about 15 km east of the city.

q.q: Until 1859, Iași was the capital of which principality?

Q5818.t: A caliphs' city on the Guadalquivir
Q5818.s: The Guadalquivir winds across a plain of olive groves and wheat, and dark hills of the Sierra Morena rise just north of the city. A thousand years ago Córdoba was the capital of a caliphate and one of the largest cities in Europe. In high summer the plain bakes: afternoon temperatures here often climb past 40 °C.
Q5818.w: A compact city on a winding river, with dark wooded hills to the north and olive groves on the plain to the south.
f: Córdoba's Great Mosque, begun in 785, has had a cathedral built inside it since the 16th century.
Medina Azahara, a ruined 10th-century palace city about 8 km west, became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2018.
The Roman bridge over the Guadalquivir was first built in the 1st century BC.

q.q: Which river flows through Córdoba?

Q2337.t: Great brick walls on the upper Dnieper
Q2337.s: Wooded hills crowd the upper Dnieper, still a modest river here, and Smolensk climbs both its banks. The city was first mentioned in 863, which makes it one of the oldest in Russia. Around 1600 it was ringed by a massive brick wall with dozens of towers, and long stretches of it still stand.
Q2337.w: A hilly city on both banks of a winding river, surrounded by forest and farmland.
f: Smolensk's fortress wall, built in 1595–1602, was about 6.5 km long with 38 towers.
The composer Mikhail Glinka was born in 1804 at Novospasskoye, an estate in the Smolensk region.
Yuri Gagarin was born in 1934 in a village in the Smolensk region.

q.q: Which river flows through Smolensk?

Q437.t: A small capital between the Alps and a marsh
Q437.s: Alpine peaks to the north, a flat marsh to the south, and Ljubljana tucked between them around a wooded castle hill. The little Ljubljanica river curls through the old town below the castle. On those southern marshes, archaeologists found prehistoric pile dwellings and a wooden wheel more than 5,000 years old.
Q437.w: A modest city around a wooded hill, flat marshland to the south and a wall of Alpine peaks to the north.
f: The Ljubljana Marshes wheel, about 5,150 years old, is one of the oldest wooden wheels ever found.
Prehistoric pile dwellings on the Ljubljana Marshes are part of a UNESCO World Heritage site.
The architect Jože Plečnik reshaped much of the city centre in the 20th century.

q.q: Which river flows through the old town of Ljubljana?

Q5265.t: A green spa town with Elbrus on the skyline
Q5265.s: The plains end abruptly at Nalchik, where the first forested ridges of the Caucasus rise. On clear days the twin white summit of Elbrus stands out to the south-west. The city's name is said to mean 'little horseshoe', after the curve of the hills around it. Parks and mineral springs have made it a spa town.
Q5265.w: A city at the edge of the plain against forested foothills, with the snowy main Caucasus ridge beyond.
f: Elbrus, the highest peak in Europe at 5,642 m, stands about 100 km to the south-west.
Nalchik is the capital of Kabardino-Balkaria.
The city's large park runs up into the forested foothills.

q.q: What does the name Nalchik mean?

Q79808.t: Ovid's place of exile, now a busy Black Sea port
Q79808.s: Long breakwaters and a maze of docks mark Romania's main gateway to the sea. North of the city, Mamaia's hotels line a narrow strip of sand between the Black Sea and a freshwater lake. In ancient times this was the Greek town of Tomis, and the Roman poet Ovid spent his last years here in exile, complaining of the cold.
Q79808.w: A port city with long breakwaters, a canal joining from the west and a thin sandbar between a lake and the sea to the north.
f: The Danube–Black Sea Canal, opened in 1984, reaches the sea just south of the city.
Constanța is Romania's largest port and one of the biggest on the Black Sea.
Mamaia resort runs along a sandbar between Lake Siutghiol and the sea.

q.q: Which Roman poet was exiled to Tomis, today's Constanța?

Q140147.t: Two railway gauges meet on a border river
Q140147.s: The Western Bug and the Mukhavets meet at Brest, and the Bug forms the border here. The land is flat, with forests and fields to the horizon. Brest is a railway crossroads where two track widths meet, Europe's standard gauge and the wider one used across the former Russian Empire, so long-distance trains change their wheel sets here.
Q140147.w: A city where two rivers meet on a flat, forested plain; the larger river runs north–south along the border.
f: Brest was first mentioned in a chronicle, as Berestye, in 1019.
At Brest, 1,435 mm standard-gauge track meets the 1,520 mm gauge used further east.
Białowieża Forest, one of the last primeval forests of Europe, lies a short way to the north.

q.q: Which river forms the border at Brest?

Q1957.t: Lace, butter and a white cathedral in the north
Q1957.s: Flat forest and marsh stretch around Vologda, and the little Vologda river loops through the middle. The city dates its founding to 1147, the same year as Moscow. Its white St Sophia Cathedral was built on the orders of Ivan the Terrible, and whole streets of carved wooden houses survive around the centre. Lake Kubenskoye glints to the north-west.
Q1957.w: A city on a small winding river in flat, forested lowland, with a long lake to the north-west.
f: Vologda lace, woven on bobbins, is one of Russia's best-known crafts.
St Sophia Cathedral in Vologda was built in 1568–1570.
Vologda butter, with its nutty taste, has a protected regional name.

q.q: What kind of lace is Vologda famous for?

Q156713.t: Granite cliffs and the birthplace of a space pioneer
Q156713.s: North of Zhytomyr the dark forests of Polesia begin, and the city spreads along the Teteriv, which cuts through outcrops of grey granite here. According to tradition, Zhytomyr was founded in 884. Its best-known son is Sergei Korolev, who became chief designer of the Soviet space programme. The city now has a museum of space flight in his name.
Q156713.w: A city on a winding river with rocky banks, farmland to the south and dark forests to the north.
f: Sergei Korolev, who led the design of the first satellite and Gagarin's rocket, was born in Zhytomyr in 1907.
The Teteriv river runs through granite cliffs in the city.
The Teteriv is a tributary of the Dnieper.

q.q: Which space pioneer was born in Zhytomyr?

Q70.t: Wrapped in a loop of glacier-green river
Q70.s: The Aare, milky green with Alpine meltwater, curls around Bern's old town in a tight loop, leaving the medieval streets on a narrow peninsula. On clear days the white wall of the Bernese Alps fills the southern horizon. Officially, Switzerland has no capital: Bern is the 'federal city', where the government and parliament sit.
Q70.w: A tight loop of a green river around a narrow old town, with snowy Alpine peaks far to the south.
f: The Old City of Bern has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1983.
Albert Einstein developed his special theory of relativity while living in Bern in 1905.
The Aare gets its green colour from fine rock flour carried down by Alpine glaciers.

q.q: Which theory did Einstein publish while living in Bern in 1905?

Q641.t: A fish-shaped city floating in a lagoon
Q641.s: In the middle of a shallow lagoon lies a tight cluster of islands shaped like a fish, cut through by one reversed S of water: the Grand Canal. That is Venice. A long straight causeway ties it to the mainland, and a chain of thin barrier islands, including the Lido, shields the lagoon from the Adriatic. Cars stop where the causeway ends; beyond, the city moves on foot and by boat.
Q641.w: A fish-shaped island city in a shallow lagoon, linked to the mainland by a long causeway, with thin barrier islands offshore.
f: Venice is built on about 118 small islands separated by canals.
The Ponte della Libertà, about 3.8 km long, carries a road and railway to the mainland.
Venice and its Lagoon have been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1987.

q.q: About how many islands is Venice built on?

Q2211.t: A bridge that dives under the sea to Denmark
Q2211.s: Out from the coast south-west of Malmö runs a fine line across the sea: the Øresund Bridge. It runs about 8 km to an artificial island, then vanishes into a tunnel for the rest of the way to Copenhagen. Malmö itself spreads over the flat, fertile farmland of Scania, Sweden's southern tip.
Q2211.w: A city on a flat coast, with a long bridge heading west over the strait to an island and Copenhagen beyond.
f: The Øresund link, opened in 2000, joins a bridge, an artificial island and a tunnel under the sea.
Turning Torso, a twisting tower about 190 m tall, was the tallest building in Scandinavia when completed in 2005.
Malmö is Sweden's third-largest city.

q.q: Which city does the Øresund link connect Malmö with?

Q1895.t: Peter's ironworks on a great northern lake
Q1895.s: Lake Onega stretches north like a scattered puzzle of bays, islands and rocky peninsulas, and Petrozavodsk lines its western shore. The city grew from an ironworks that Peter the Great founded in 1703 to cast cannon, and its name simply means 'Peter's works'. Out on the lake lies Kizhi island, famous for its wooden churches.
Q1895.w: A city along the curved shore of a huge lake, with long bays and forested peninsulas reaching north.
f: Lake Onega is the second-largest lake in Europe, after Ladoga.
Kizhi's wooden churches, north-east of the city on the lake, are a UNESCO World Heritage site.
The ironworks that gave the city its name was founded in 1703.

q.q: On which lake does Petrozavodsk stand?

Q40840.t: A factory town between two lakes
Q40840.s: Two big lakes nearly touch at Tampere, and the city fills the narrow neck between them. Water pours from the northern lake to the southern one down the Tammerkoski rapids, and that drop powered the first factories in the 19th century. Red-brick mills made this the 'Manchester of Finland'. All around, forest and lakes stretch into the distance.
Q40840.w: A city on a narrow strip of land between a large lake to the north and another to the south.
f: The Tammerkoski rapids fall about 18 m between lakes Näsijärvi and Pyhäjärvi.
Scottish engineer James Finlayson founded a cotton mill beside the rapids in 1820.
Tampere is the largest inland city in the Nordic countries.

q.q: What connects Tampere's two big lakes?

Q103565.t: A planned city on the river that leaves Baikal
Q103565.s: Angarsk was laid out from 1948 as a planned city, and its neat grid of blocks still stands out between the Angara and the Kitoy. On its edge sprawls one of Siberia's biggest refinery and chemical complexes. The Angara here has only recently left Lake Baikal, and the city of Irkutsk lies a short way upstream.
Q103565.w: A neat grid of blocks between two rivers, with a large industrial complex alongside and taiga beyond.
f: Construction of Angarsk began in 1948, and it became a city in 1951.
The Angara is the only river that flows out of Lake Baikal.
Angarsk has a museum devoted entirely to clocks.

q.q: Which river flows out of Lake Baikal past Angarsk?

Q42810.t: The harbour that gave Impressionism its name
Q42810.s: The Seine ends in a wide estuary, and Le Havre guards its northern shore. Look for the fine line of the Pont de Normandie arching across the river mouth. The city was founded in 1517 by King Francis I as a port. In 1872 Claude Monet painted its harbour at dawn, and the title, 'Impression, Sunrise', gave a whole art movement its name.
Q42810.w: A port city on the northern shore of a wide estuary, with long docks and a slender bridge across the river mouth.
f: Auguste Perret's concrete city centre has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2005.
The Pont de Normandie, opened in 1995, is a cable-stayed bridge more than 2 km long.
Le Havre is one of France's busiest container ports.

q.q: Which painting of Le Havre gave Impressionism its name?

Q5196.t: An oil city on the Sunzha below the Caucasus
Q5196.s: The plain north of the Caucasus is crossed here by the Sunzha, and Grozny spreads along its banks with low ridges rising to the north. On the southern horizon, forested foothills climb towards the snowy main range. The city began in 1818 as a Russian fortress, and oil made it grow: wells were drilled here in the 1890s, among the earliest in the empire.
Q5196.w: A large city on a river crossing a plain, low ridges to the north and forested mountains rising to the south.
f: Grozny was founded in 1818 as the fortress of Groznaya on the Sunzha river.
Industrial oil production around Grozny began in the 1890s.
The Sunzha is a tributary of the Terek, which it joins east of the city.

q.q: On which river does Grozny stand?

Q6934.t: A city on each bank of the Amur, in two countries
Q6934.s: Two countries, two cities, one river: across the Amur from Blagoveshchensk, less than a kilometre away, stands Heihe in China. At night their lights face each other over the dark water. Blagoveshchensk began in 1856 as a military post where the Zeya pours into the Amur, and flat, fertile farmland of the Amur region spreads all around it.
Q6934.w: Two cities facing each other across a wide river, where a large tributary joins from the north; flat farmland all around.
f: The Chinese city of Heihe lies directly across the Amur, less than a kilometre away.
The city's name means 'Annunciation', after its first church.
The Zeya, which joins the Amur here, is more than 1,200 km long.

q.q: Which river joins the Amur at Blagoveshchensk?

Q2214.t: A stone kremlin on a spit between two rivers
Q2214.s: On a rocky spit where the little Pskova joins the broad Velikaya rises the Krom, Pskov's kremlin, and the city spreads around it on both banks. A short way downstream the Velikaya flows into Lake Pskov, the southern part of the vast Lake Peipus. Pskov was first mentioned in 903, making it one of Russia's oldest cities.
Q2214.w: A city on a broad river flowing north-west into a huge lake, with a smaller river joining in the centre.
f: Pskov was first mentioned in the chronicles in 903.
The churches of the Pskov school of architecture became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2019.
Lake Peipus, into which the Velikaya flows, is one of the largest lakes in Europe.

q.q: Which river flows past the Pskov Krom?

Q7859.t: A ski slope right above an island capital
Q7859.s: A ski slope drops almost into the eastern streets of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, which lines a long valley between two ranges of forested mountains near the southern end of Sakhalin. To the south the valley opens onto Aniva Bay, where the port of Korsakov sits. Sakhalin is Russia's largest island, and its southern tip is only about 40 km from Japan's Hokkaido.
Q7859.w: A long city in a green valley between two forested mountain ranges, opening south to a wide bay.
f: Sakhalin, about 950 km long, is the largest island in Russia.
Russia's first liquefied natural gas plant opened in 2009 at Prigorodnoye on Aniva Bay.
The Gorny Vozdukh ski area rises right at the city's eastern edge.

q.q: Which bay lies south of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk?

Q875.t: A steppe capital among ancient burial mounds
Q875.s: In a wide basin ringed by the Sayan and Kuznetsk Alatau mountains, the Abakan river joins the mighty Yenisei, and the city of Abakan stands in the angle between them. The basin is open steppe, warm by Siberian standards, and scattered with ancient burial mounds and standing stones. Across the Yenisei lies the older town of Minusinsk.
Q875.w: A city where a river joins a much bigger one in open steppe, with mountains far around the basin.
f: Abakan is the capital of Khakassia.
Abakan received city status only in 1931.
The Minusinsk Basin around Abakan is rich in ancient kurgans, standing stones and rock carvings.

q.q: Which great river does the Abakan join here?

Q175517.t: The biggest city this far north, cut off from roads
Q175517.s: No city of more than 100,000 people lies farther north than Norilsk, set in bare tundra near the foot of the Putorana Plateau. No road or railway links it to the rest of Russia: people fly in, and freight comes up the Yenisei to the port of Dudinka. Much of the year the land is white, and from early December the sun does not rise for weeks.
Q175517.w: A compact city and huge smelters on white or brown tundra, with lakes and the dark cliffs of a plateau to the east.
f: Norilsk is the world's leading producer of palladium, a metal used in car exhaust catalysts.
The Putorana Plateau, rising east of the city, has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2010.
A short railway links Norilsk only with Dudinka, its port on the Yenisei.

q.q: Norilsk is the world's leading producer of which metal?

Q23564.t: A hot capital between canyons and a great lake
Q23564.s: Mountains wall in Podgorica on three sides, while to the south the flat Zeta plain runs down to Lake Skadar, the largest lake in the Balkans. The Morača river cuts through the city in a rocky channel and is joined here by the Ribnica. The name means 'below Gorica', after the small wooded hill beside the centre.
Q23564.w: A city on a flat plain ringed by bare mountains, with a river gorge through it and a large lake to the south.
f: Lake Skadar, shared by Montenegro and Albania, is the largest lake in the Balkans.
Summer afternoons in Podgorica often pass 35 °C.
North of the city, the Morača has carved a canyon hundreds of metres deep.

q.q: What does the name Podgorica mean?

Q6049.t: The claimed centre of Asia, where the Yenisei is born
Q6049.s: Two mountain rivers, the Big and Little Yenisei, meet at Kyzyl and flow on together as the Yenisei, one of the longest rivers on Earth. Around the city spreads a dry basin of steppe, ringed by the mountains of Tuva. On the riverbank an obelisk marks what is claimed to be the geographical centre of Asia. The name Kyzyl simply means 'red'.
Q6049.w: A small city where two rivers meet, in a dry steppe basin ringed by mountains.
f: The Biy-Khem and the Kaa-Khem, the Big and Little Yenisei, join at Kyzyl.
Kyzyl is the capital of Tuva, a republic famous for throat singing.
The Arzhan burial mounds in Tuva held some of the richest Scythian-era gold ever found.

q.q: What is said to lie at Kyzyl?

Q1842.t: A fortress city on cliffs above deep gorges
Q1842.s: Sheer cliffs drop from Luxembourg's old town, on its rocky plateau, into the green gorges of the Alzette and the Pétrusse. Its fortifications were once so formidable that it was called the Gibraltar of the North. East of the old town, the Kirchberg plateau carries European institutions, and all around lie the rolling woods and fields of a small country.
Q1842.w: A city cut by deep, green river gorges, with an old town on a rocky plateau and new districts on a plateau to the east.
f: Luxembourg's old quarters and fortifications have been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1994.
The Bock casemates, tunnels carved into the rock, once ran for about 23 km.
Luxembourg, with Brussels and Strasbourg, is one of the main seats of European Union institutions.

q.q: What nickname did Luxembourg's fortress earn?

Q196946.t: A dam town where the Ilim meets the Angara
Q196946.s: Taiga runs unbroken to the horizon, and through it the Angara has been turned into a long, branching reservoir. At its lower end stands the Ust-Ilimsk dam, and beside it the town, built from the late 1960s. Its name means 'mouth of the Ilim': the reservoir drowned the lower valley of that river too, reaching deep into the forest.
Q196946.w: A long, many-armed reservoir in endless taiga, with a straight dam across the river and a town beside it.
f: The Ust-Ilimsk hydroelectric station on the Angara has a capacity of about 3,840 MW.
The Ust-Ilimsk reservoir stretches for hundreds of kilometres up the Angara and the Ilim.
Timber and pulp from the surrounding taiga are the town's other main industry.

q.q: What does 'Ust' mean in the name Ust-Ilimsk?

Q133529.t: A coal town in the tundra with no road out
Q133529.s: About 100 km beyond the Arctic Circle, in open tundra near the Polar Urals, stands Vorkuta. No road connects it to the rest of Russia; the railway is its lifeline. Coal mines are scattered around it, and a ring road links the city with a chain of mining settlements. In winter the sun disappears for weeks.
Q133529.w: A small city on white or brown tundra, linked by a looping road to outlying settlements, with mountains to the east.
f: Vorkuta is one of the largest towns north of the Arctic Circle in Europe.
The Pechora coal basin around Vorkuta produces high-quality coking coal.

q.q: What is mined around Vorkuta?

Q26476.t: A stone town between two hills on a Baltic bay
Q26476.s: Two steep, wooded hills stand guard over Sundsvall, which fills the gap between them at the head of a bay on the Gulf of Bothnia. In the 19th century the coast here was lined with sawmills, and timber made the town rich. Its centre, rebuilt in stone in the 1890s, is still called Stenstaden, 'the stone town'. Alnö island lies just offshore to the east.
Q26476.w: A town at the head of a bay between two wooded hills, with a large island just offshore.
f: In the late 19th century, dozens of sawmills made the Sundsvall area one of the world's great timber exporters.
The stone-built centre, Stenstaden, dates from the 1890s.
The High Coast, a UNESCO site known for rapid land uplift, lies a short way to the north.

q.q: What made Sundsvall rich in the 19th century?

Q2415.t: Norway's southern tip, laid out by a king
Q2415.s: A tangle of rocky skerries and pine-clad islets fringes the coast at Kristiansand, near Norway's southern tip. The town was founded in 1641 by King Christian IV, who gave it his name and a strict grid of square blocks, still visible in the centre. Ferries leave from here across the Skagerrak to Denmark.
Q2415.w: A small gridded town on a rocky coast full of islets, with forested hills behind.
f: Kristiansand's centre, Kvadraturen, keeps the square grid laid out in 1641.
Ferries link Kristiansand with Hirtshals in Denmark, across the Skagerrak.
Kristiansand is the largest city of Sørlandet, Norway's southern coast.

q.q: Which king founded Kristiansand in 1641?

Q208149.t: A mid-Atlantic port beside blue and green crater lakes
Q208149.s: São Miguel rises alone from the middle of the Atlantic, and Ponta Delgada lines its southern shore. West of the city, look for a great round crater holding two lakes side by side, one blue and one green: Sete Cidades. The island is patched with green pastures and hedges of blue hydrangeas.
Q208149.w: A white town along the south coast of a green volcanic island, with a large crater holding two lakes to the north-west.
f: São Miguel is the largest island of the Azores.
Tea has been grown on São Miguel since the 19th century, one of the few tea plantations in Europe.
The Sete Cidades crater, about 5 km across, lies about 15 km north-west of the city.

q.q: On which island does Ponta Delgada stand?

Q125080.t: A coast where the land keeps rising from the sea
Q125080.s: Off Vaasa, the sea is scattered with thousands of low islands and skerries, and every year there is a little more land. Freed from the weight of the Ice Age glaciers, the ground here still rises by several millimetres a year, so new islets surface and bays turn into meadows. The Kvarken archipelago is a UNESCO site for this very reason.
Q125080.w: A coastal town facing a sea filled with countless low, rocky islands, with flat farmland inland.
f: The land around Vaasa rises about 8 mm a year as it rebounds from the Ice Age.
The Replot Bridge, about 1 km long, is the longest bridge in Finland.
The Kvarken Archipelago shares a UNESCO listing with Sweden's High Coast.

q.q: Why is new land slowly appearing off Vaasa?

Q1863.t: Europe's highest capital, deep in the Pyrenees
Q1863.s: Steep Pyrenean slopes, snowy for much of the year, leave room only for a narrow valley, and Andorra la Vella fills its floor along the Gran Valira river. At about 1,023 m above sea level, it is the highest capital city in Europe. From the air the whole country looks tiny: a knot of mountain valleys between France and Spain.
Q1863.w: A narrow town squeezed along a mountain valley floor, surrounded by high, often snowy Pyrenean ridges.
f: Andorra la Vella lies at about 1,023 m, the highest of Europe's capitals.
Andorra has two co-princes: the Bishop of Urgell and the President of France.
Andorra covers about 468 km².

q.q: Who is Andorra's co-prince alongside the Bishop of Urgell?

Q26268.t: A town that moved to follow the sea
Q26268.s: The Lule river meets the Gulf of Bothnia among an archipelago of more than a thousand islands, and Luleå sits on a peninsula in their midst. The town moved here in 1649: the land was rising so fast after the Ice Age that its old harbour had become too shallow. In winter the sea freezes, and roads are ploughed across the ice to the islands.
Q26268.w: A town on a peninsula at a river mouth, surrounded by a maze of forested islands in a shallow sea.
f: Gammelstad, the old church town with more than 400 wooden cottages, is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
The Luleå archipelago has about 1,300 islands.
In winter, ice roads are ploughed across the frozen sea to some of the islands.

q.q: Why did Luleå move to a new site in 1649?
q.a: Rising land made the harbour too shallow
x: The king wanted a sea fortress

Q105477.t: A giant diamond pit at the edge of town
Q105477.s: Look for a vast round hole beside the town, its sides spiralling down in terraces: the Mir mine, one of the largest man-made pits on Earth. Diamond-bearing rock was found here in 1955, and the town of Mirny grew up in the Yakutian taiga beside it. In winter the temperature here can drop below −40 °C.
Q105477.w: A huge round pit with terraced sides at the edge of a small town, in endless taiga.
f: The Mir pit is about 525 m deep and about 1.2 km across.
Mirny is the centre of Russia's diamond industry.
Open-pit mining at Mir ended in 2001; mining continued underground.

q.q: What was mined in the great pit at Mirny?

Q235.t: A whole country squeezed onto a strip of coast
Q235.s: Between the mountains and the sea, a tiny country packs itself into a strip of coast only a few kilometres long. Monaco's towers crowd around a harbour full of yachts, and some districts stand on land reclaimed from the Mediterranean. Behind it, bare limestone slopes rise steeply towards the Alps, and France surrounds it on every landward side.
Q235.w: A dense strip of towers around a small harbour on a steep coast, between the sea and bare mountains.
f: At about 2 km², Monaco is the world's second-smallest country, after Vatican City.
The Grimaldi family has ruled Monaco, with interruptions, since 1297.
The Fontvieille district was built on land reclaimed from the sea.

q.q: Which is the only country smaller than Monaco?

Q1844.t: A tiny capital on the Rhine, twice cut off from the sea
Q1844.s: Straight and wide, the Rhine runs down a flat-floored Alpine valley here, marking the border with Switzerland. On its eastern side, Vaduz spreads along the foot of steep, forested mountains, with the prince's castle perched on a ledge above. Liechtenstein itself is only about 25 km long, so from cruise height the whole country fits in a single glance.
Q1844.w: A small town beside a straight, broad river in a flat Alpine valley, backed by steep forested slopes.
f: Liechtenstein is one of only two doubly landlocked countries in the world; the other is Uzbekistan.
Liechtenstein covers about 160 km².
Vaduz Castle, above the town, is the residence of the Prince of Liechtenstein.

q.q: Which other country is, like Liechtenstein, doubly landlocked?

Q103717.t: Lapland's capital, a stone's throw from the Arctic Circle
Q103717.s: The Kemijoki and the Ounasjoki, two big rivers, meet at Rovaniemi amid endless pine forest and bog. The Arctic Circle runs only about 8 km north of the centre, and a whole tourist village has grown up on the line itself, home to Santa Claus. In December the sun barely clears the horizon, and the northern lights often flicker overhead.
Q103717.w: A town where two wide rivers meet in flat, forested country, snow-covered for about half the year.
f: Santa Claus Village stands right on the Arctic Circle, about 8 km north of the centre.
Alvar Aalto's town plan lays out Rovaniemi's main roads in the shape of a reindeer's head and antlers.
The Kemijoki, which flows through the town, is Finland's longest river.

q.q: Whose official 'village' stands on the Arctic Circle near Rovaniemi?

Q1848.t: The world's oldest republic, on a three-towered ridge
Q1848.s: A lone limestone ridge rears up from the rolling hills behind the Adriatic coast: Monte Titano, crowned by three towers and the old town of San Marino. The whole country, about 61 km², is surrounded by Italy. Tradition says a stonemason named Marinus founded a community here in 301, which would make it the oldest surviving republic in the world.
Q1848.w: A steep, isolated ridge with a town along its crest, rising from green hills a short way inland from the Adriatic coast.
f: Monte Titano rises to 739 m, with three medieval towers along its ridge.
San Marino covers about 61 km² and is entirely surrounded by Italy.
The historic centre and Monte Titano became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2008.

q.q: According to tradition, in which year was San Marino founded?

Q177782.s: Near the northern end of Sakhalin, the island flattens into a low, boggy plain of larch woods and lakes, and Okha grew up among the oil fields there. Oil seeping from the ground was noticed in the 19th century. The town's name is thought to come from an Evenki word meaning 'bad', after the oily, undrinkable water of the local river.
Q177782.w: A small town on a flat, boggy plain near the northern tip of a long, narrow island, with oil fields around it.
f: The Okha oil field was discovered in 1880, and industrial production began in 1921.
Okha received town status in 1938.
Okha is the northernmost town on Sakhalin.

q.q: What resource did Okha grow up around?

Q157493.t: A Lena river port feeding the diamond fields
Q157493.s: Wide and brown, the Lena winds through the Yakutian taiga, and Lensk strings out along its bank.
